items.blurb: A little more than four years ago, humans moved an asteroid, as NASA’s DART spacecraft impacted a body called Dimorphos. Now the European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft has arrived at that same asteroid to find out what happened next. Join the Hera team on the evening of Wednesday 25 November as they share the first close-up images of this historic transformed space object.

items.blurb: The Voyager spacecraft get closer to Earth for a few months every year. Will Voyager 1 cross back under the 1 light-day distance? The post Will Voyager 1 ever be closer than 1 light-day from Earth again? first appeared on EarthSky .

items.blurb: NASA astronaut and commander of the agency’s Artemis II mission, Reid Wiseman, a Baltimore native, takes a selfie with fans at an NFL game between the New Orleans Saints and the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium, Sunday, Sept. 20, 2026, in Baltimore.

items.blurb: Researchers in the Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences (SEAS) have engineered an advancement in metasurface design and processing that now includes a built-in, intentionally designed antireflective coating—a potentially critical step toward greatly expanding the incorporation of metasurfaces into practical devices.

items.title: UN climate talks enter crunch time with no deal in sight
items.blurb: The U.N.'s COP31 climate talks enter their endgame Friday, with countries sharply divided over a draft deal lacking any mention of planet-heating fossil fuels, threatening to push the negotiations into overtime.

items.title: Fiona the hippo dies after failed effort to remove swallowed hat
items.blurb: World-famous hippopotamus Fiona has died after several failed attempts by vets to remove a woolly hat that she accidentally swallowed, the Cincinnati Zoo announced Thursday.

items.title: Nature's multilayered defenses against crop pests and viruses revealed
items.blurb: Researchers from the University of Nottingham, in collaboration with Syngenta and Keele University, have discovered how a commercial barley hybrid uses three complementary natural defenses to protect itself against aphids and the damaging viruses they spread. The findings could help breeders develop crops with stronger natural protection against pests and diseases.

items.title: The BepiColombo spacecraft is finally entering orbit around Mercury
items.blurb: After an eight-year voyage towards the sun, the BepiColombo spacecraft can finally begin its mission to unpick the many mysteries of our solar system's smallest planet

items.title: computor: AI tutor as a programming learning aid
items.blurb: Artificial intelligence is now capable of writing entire computer programs. This poses a challenge for university education. How can students still learn to program for themselves if an AI can do the work for them? Students should be able to use AI tools effectively, but they must also understand how programs work and how to troubleshoot errors. At the Institute of Theoretical and Computational Physics at Graz University of Technology (TU Graz), a team led by Christopher Albert has developed the "computor" learning platform for this purpose. The system is already being used in teaching and is available to the public.

items.title: How nature-based solutions are failing informal settlements
items.blurb: New research from UCT says nature-based solutions for climate adaptation must move beyond participation to power-sharing partnerships that recognize lived experiences and relationships with nature.

items.title: Extreme weather poses growing risks to global oil and natural gas shipping, new IEA report finds
items.blurb: Extreme weather events are posing significant risks to international oil and natural gas shipping, with the potential to damage critical infrastructure, disrupt major trade routes and threaten energy security, according to a new IEA report.

items.title: AI virtual cell technology could reveal how genetic changes and drugs alter cells
items.blurb: Today's artificial intelligence models can predict whether someone with a genetic change will develop a disease, but cannot answer two critical questions: Why did the disease occur, and how do we design a treatment?

items.title: Building structured-light systems in three dimensions
items.blurb: Structured light has become an important tool across modern optics. By shaping properties such as amplitude, phase, polarization and spatial mode, researchers can create light fields with capabilities beyond those of conventional laser beams. These engineered light fields are finding applications in communications, imaging, sensing, optical computing and quantum photonics. However, many structured-light systems still rely on multiple discrete optical components that require careful alignment and occupy significant space.

items.title: Innovative technology offers a bold new vision for monitoring ocean health
items.blurb: On an early October morning, as MBARI's research vessel Paragon left Moss Landing with three robots loaded on its deck, Monterey Bay was showing off.

items.blurb: Botanists have described a new Ophiopogon species from the Yunnan Wenshan National Nature Reserve in southeastern China. They named it Ophiopogon longiscapus for its unusually long flowering stalk, or scape.

items.title: Organizational science offers new lens for studying extremism
items.blurb: Accepting the Republican nomination for president in 1964, Barry Goldwater declared, "I would remind you that extremism in the defense of liberty is no vice!" His statement illustrates how the cause being defended can shape judgments about the actions taken in its name.

items.title: New study: The last bird to go extinct in NZ has lessons for saving other species
items.blurb: The last bird to go extinct in Aotearoa New Zealand was a tiny wren that disappeared from a small island off the southern tip of Rakiura Stewart Island around 1972.

items.title: Climate communication that resonates must be based on empathy
items.blurb: Climate change is a global reality, but people often encounter it through different local realities. For some, it enters everyday life through social media feeds, news reports, scientific findings and public discussion. For others, it is through water scarcity, food insecurity, floods, heat waves, wildfires or the loss of a home or a loved one.

items.title: Putting Google's AI hurricane model to the test
items.blurb: A week before Hurricane Melissa slammed into Jamaica last fall, the forecast models couldn't agree on where it was headed or how strong it would get. One got it right—an AI model from Google DeepMind, which called both the storm's path and its Category 5 strength.

items.blurb: AI companions could help reduce loneliness by creating a greater sense of belonging and improving self-esteem, according to new research from Durham University Business School.

items.title: Q&A: Making hydrogen peroxide without using precious metals
items.blurb: Hydrogen peroxide is used in many industrial processes, with several million tons of it being manufactured worldwide every year. Whereas the standard production method requires rare precious metals, chemists from Rutgers University–Newark in the US and the University of Bonn have now described an alternative technique that does away with these metals, making it potentially cheaper and more sustainable. Their findings have now been published in the journal Nature Communications. In the following interview, the authors describe the technology.

items.title: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle
items.blurb: Researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a compound that could transform weight-loss treatment by helping the body burn more energy instead of suppressing appetite like Ozempic and Wegovy. In mice, the compound boosted energy expenditure by up to 18%, improved blood sugar control, reduced liver fat, and promoted weight loss without significant muscle loss. Even more promising, combining it with existing GLP-1 medications produced greater benefits than either treatment alone.

items.title: Can AI save peer review from AI?

items.title: Spatial organization of a SPINK1-associated tumor-stromal ecosystem links metabolic remodeling to immune restriction in bladder cancer
items.blurb: Spatially organized tumor-stromal interactions contribute to metabolic remodeling and immune suppression in bladder cancer (BLCA). Using spatial transcriptional programs to define single-cell states, we identified a niche comprising SPINK1-high epithelial cells (E2) and TPM2-high cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) (C1). SPINK1 promoted tumor growth and myofibroblastic CAF programs, with EGFR and TGF-{beta} signaling implicated in tumor-CAF communication. Inferred metabolic reactions and spatial metabolite distributions supported a candidate circuit linking tumor-derived lactate to CAF oxidative metabolism and glutamine provision, followed by tumor glutamine utilization for reductive carboxylation and fatty acid synthesis. SPINK1 perturbation altered extracellular glutamine and lactate concentrations. Predicted chemokine interactions implicated C2/C3 CAFs in T cell recruitment, whereas the E2-C1 niche exhibited checkpoint and exhaustion-associated features. RHCG-positive tumor regions contained higher proportions of TOXCXCR4 cells among CD3 T cells, suggesting a possible association between ammonia handling and T cell dysfunction. In vivo, Spink1 loss attenuated tumor progression, increased cytotoxic CD8 T-cell infiltration, and enhanced tumor control during PD-1 blockade. These findings identify a spatially organized tumor-stromal niche associated with metabolic cooperation and immune restriction, supporting SPINK1 as a candidate therapeutic target in combination with immunotherapy.

items.title: The tumor suppressor role of the KRAS proto-oncogene in metastatic pancreatic cancer.
items.blurb: KRAS is the most frequently mutated proto-oncogene in human cancers. Progression to advanced disease is frequently associated with allelic imbalance of the KRAS locus with gain of the mutant allele and loss of the wild-type allele through clonal and sub-clonal loss of heterozygosity (LOH). While a large body of literature has focused on the effects of allelic imbalance on oncogene addiction through gain of the mutant allele, the role of the wild-type KRAS proto-oncogene in malignant progression has not been fully elucidated. To capture this phenomenon, we developed a first-in-class somatic mosaic and lineage tracing genetically engineered mouse model (smGMLT) of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma allowing for real time in vivo tracing of Kras-LOH. Longitudinal characterization of the smGMLT demonstrated the presence of a strong evolutionary bottleneck towards the selective loss of the wild-type allele at metastatic sites. Cross species analysis leveraging research autopsies and surgical specimens revealed that KRAS-LOH is associated with metastatic dissemination and shorter overall survival. Transcriptomic analysis through single-cell RNA sequencing uncovered a conserved phenomenon whereby KRAS-LOH is paralleled by an immune evasive phenotype through loss of the tumor-cell interferon response and reduced CD8+ T cell infiltration. In line with this evidence, orthotopic transplants of isogenic tumor populations differing for the Kras allelic status demonstrated that only cancer cells with Kras-LOH are are able to form tumors in immune competent animals. Restoration of the wild-type allele abrogates tumorigenesis in KrasLOH transplants in immunocompetent through activation of the TBK1-IRF axis. Altogether, these studies demonstrate that the KRAS proto-oncogene is a functional tumor suppressor in pancreatic cancer exerting its function through interferon-mediated, cell-extrinsic modulation of the tumor immune microenvironment.

items.title: CELL-X: A Single-Cell Transcriptomics Framework for Cell-Type and Disease-State Prioritization of Type 2 Diabetes Risk Genes
items.blurb: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci associated with Type 2 Diabetes (T2D), yet pinpointing specific causal genes and their relevant cellular contexts remains a critical bottleneck. To address this gap, we developed CELL-X, a novel computational framework systematically integrating fine-mapped genetic evidence with high-resolution single-cell transcriptomics and disease progression dynamics. Utilizing a custom out-of-memory processing engine, we analyzed an integrated human pancreatic islet atlas of 245,878 cells without forced data downsampling. We evaluated 37 genetically supported T2D candidate genes, quantifying cell-type relevance via a max-scaled Cell Relevance Score (CRS). Disease-associated transcriptional dynamics were subsequently incorporated using a Disease Relevance Score (DRS) based on heterogeneous expression shifts across normal, prediabetic, and T2D metabolic states. CELL-X successfully identified beta cells as the dominant disease-relevant cellular context and prioritized established causal genes, including SLC30A8, GLIS3, GCK, and TCF7L2. Validation against a 30-gene benchmark demonstrated exceptional target recovery and significant metabolic pathway enrichment. Furthermore, rigorous statistical null modeling confirmed this prioritization is driven by true biological variance rather than background transcriptomic noise. Ultimately, CELL-X provides a highly scalable, robust framework for generating biologically informed hypotheses in complex polygenic disease research.

items.title: SNP2Cluster-Py: A pathogen-agnostic, context-aware framework for Core SNP and transmission-cluster analysis
items.blurb: Whole-genome sequencing enables high-resolution identification of genetically related pathogen isolates, but genomic similarity alone does not establish epidemiologically meaningful transmission. We developed SNP2Cluster-Py, an open-source Python framework that separates context-aware Core SNP clustering from the subsequent application of epidemiological and temporal criteria. The software accepts a precomputed pairwise Core SNP-distance matrix and user-configured metadata and supports analysis of all eligible isolates in a single context, as well as sequence-type, geographical, epidemiological and ordered composite contexts. Within each context, authoritative Core clusters are defined as connected components of an SNP-threshold graph; K-means assignments and silhouette widths are retained as exploratory diagnostics only. We evaluated the workflow using 172 Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates from six neonatal-surveillance hospitals in South Africa, a focused 36-isolate single-hospital subset from the same surveillance dataset, and 168 Streptococcus pneumoniae carriage isolates from Ghana. In the full K. pneumoniae dataset, ST-only analysis assigned 141 isolates to Core SNP clusters, whereas Facility + ST analysis assigned 134, demonstrating how facility stratification can remove cross-facility genomic connections. In the single-hospital subset, both contexts assigned 30 of 36 isolates to five Core clusters, and Facility analysis retained 23 isolates in four temporally compatible clusters. In the pneumococcal dataset, ST-context analysis assigned 114 isolates to 38 Core clusters, which were characterised across sampling locations and time through Community analysis. SNP2Cluster-Py therefore provides a reproducible framework for adapting genomic clustering to specific surveillance questions while maintaining a clear distinction between genomic relatedness, analytically inferred transmission clusters and confirmed direct transmission. SNP2Cluster-Py v1.1.2 is available under the Apache License 2.0 through GitHub and Zenodo.

items.title: Learning RNA secondary structure from chemical probing with MXfold2
items.blurb: Training RNA secondary structure predictors is limited by scarce reference annotations, even as chemical probing produces abundant nucleotide-level measurements. These measurements inform pairing states without identifying base-pairing partners. Here we extend MXfold2, which combines neural and thermodynamic folding scores, to learn from probing profiles and predict RNA secondary structures from sequence alone. We introduce three training objectives. One learns from probing-assisted target structures. The other two use implicit maximum-likelihood estimation to pass surrogate gradients from reactivity-ranking and likelihood losses through discrete folding. Simulations, RNAgym measurements and external structural tests show improved chemical agreement and gains in exact base-pair prediction when chemical supervision is combined with structural pretraining and replay. Probing profiles can thus broaden the range of RNAs that inform sequence-only structure prediction, including RNA populations with few complete structure annotations.

items.title: NeuroSim: a clinically informed multi-disorder EEG simulator with personalized pattern injection and AI-driven neurological modeling
items.blurb: Deep learning for electroencephalography (EEG) based neurodiagnostics is constrained by the limited availability of labeled clinical recordings. Datasets covering Alzheimers disease (AD), Parkinsons disease (PD), schizophrenia (SCZ), epilepsy (EPI), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are scarce, demographically narrow, and heterogeneous across acquisition sites, while privacy requirements restrict data sharing. Existing EEG simulators typically address a single disorder or trade biological interpretability for statistical fidelity. This study presents NeuroSim, a simulation framework that generates synthetic multichannel EEG with user-controlled injection of disease-specific patterns across five disorders and multiple severity levels. A physiologically motivated baseline generator produces band-limited rhythms, event-related potentials, artifacts, and hierarchical subject-level and trial-level variability. Disease patterns are introduced through region-specific and severity-specific spectral modulation that encodes established biomarkers, including posterior alpha suppression in AD, motor beta enhancement in PD, and spike-wave discharges in EPI. An interactive interface exposes montage, sampling rate, duration, artifacts, stimuli, affected regions, and severity, and exports signals with reproducible metadata. The simulated signals reproduced the expected biomarker directionality under spectral, topographic, and multivariate statistical analysis. A convolutional-attention classifier trained on simulated data reached 95.3 to 96.8 percent hold-out accuracy, and post hoc explainability analyses produced class-separable embeddings with attributions concentrated on pathophysiologically expected electrodes. Application of the analysis pipeline to recordings from the Temple University Hospital EEG Corpus confirmed compatibility with heterogeneous clinical data. In subject-level augmentation experiments on real clinical EEG, supplementing real training data with NeuroSim samples increased classification accuracy from 91.6 to 94.5 percent for AD versus healthy controls and from 90.9 to 94.0 percent for PD versus healthy controls, exceeding the improvement obtained with conventional signal-level augmentation. NeuroSim is released as open-source software to support augmentation, benchmarking, and explainable artificial intelligence in neurological diagnostics.

items.title: Identification of SAMD4B as a Centrosome-Associated Regulator of the Sonic Hedgehog Signaling Pathway
items.blurb: Background: Many protein-protein interactions are required for the assembly and function of primary cilia, microtubule-based organelles critical for the Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signaling pathway and, in turn, for embryonic development and tissue homeostasis. However, our understanding of this complex process remains incomplete. Methods: To identify new regulators of primary cilia formation or function, we carried out proximity labeling experiments and compared interactomes under ciliogenesis-restrictive and permissive conditions. Using an unbiased strategy, we selected candidates that were tested functionally by siRNA-mediated depletion or gene editing, in combination with gene expression analysis and various microscopy techniques, using either vertebrate cell lines or zebrafish as model systems. Results: We demonstrate that one of our identified candidates, protein SAMD4B, is associated with the centrosome and is required for Shh signaling in NIH3T3 cells and eye development in zebrafish. Our data implicate defective ciliary recruitment of Shh pathway regulators ARL13B and SMO as a plausible mechanism underlying the SAMD4B-mediated regulation of Shh signaling. Conclusions: Together, our data identify a previously unrecognized link between SAMD4B, a protein known to be associated with cytoplasmic RNA condensates, and ciliary signaling.

items.title: 'PAC-MAN' capsules that gobble up particles in turbulent water show promise for filtration and drug delivery
items.blurb: Scientists have created hollow capsules with single openings that can selectively filter particles thanks to the turbulence in surrounding waters—at times, ingesting particles like PAC-MAN eating up dots.

items.title: Britain should treat healthy seas as essential infrastructure, say scientists
items.blurb: Researchers are calling for lasting investment in healthy seas to support food security, protect coastlines and strengthen economic resilience.

items.title: The secret of 'strange metals' may lie in quantum statistics, not collisions
items.blurb: In an ordinary metal, electrons behave like well-defined particles that occasionally bump into imperfections or vibrations of the crystal. Many materials with strong electron–electron interactions, including the copper-oxide (cuprate) superconductors, break these rules. In these "strange metals," electrical resistance rises in a straight line with temperature over a very wide range. Electrons seem to lose their momentum at the fastest rate quantum mechanics allows, the so-called Planckian limit. What causes this is still an open question.

items.title: Euclid's hunt for strong gravitational lenses is off to a strong start
items.blurb: If dark matter and dark energy were a part of our everyday lives, we would live in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness. Imagine living in a world where 95% of the matter and energy were invisible and undetectable. It would be impossible to make sense of our surroundings.

items.title: Staying alive in marsh muck: The tiny 'snorkels' cattails grow manipulate soil chemistry
items.blurb: Cattails are a familiar sight in wetlands, where they thrive in both brackish and freshwater marshes. But surviving in waterlogged soil presents a challenge; their roots need oxygen in an environment where very little is available.

items.title: Dual-purpose polymer dots could combine bioimaging and light-triggered cell death in one material
items.blurb: A research team led by professor Youhei Takeda at the University of Osaka, in collaboration with professor Zachary M. Hudson at the University of British Columbia (UBC) in Canada, has developed a polymer material that combines fluorescent cell imaging with the potential to kill cancer cells when activated by light. The material could offer a simpler approach to developing "nanotheranostic" technologies, which bring disease imaging and treatment together in a single platform.

items.title: Individual meerkats are ace solo navigators
items.blurb: After meerkats emerge each morning from their burrow to warm in the early sun, there's one thing on their collective mind, and that's to find food. They navigate communally as they head off, working slowly along their route before returning home swiftly at the end of the day. But although the tight-knit band navigates as one, some members of the clan could be more experienced after roaming solo, shaping the community's maneuvers.

items.title: How microbes make drug-like chemicals without damaging themselves
items.blurb: University of Michigan researchers have discovered a mechanism that enables microscopic organisms like bacteria and fungi to produce drug-like molecules—compounds that can fight infections or kill cancer cells—without damaging themselves.

items.title: ESA's Hera probe uses 'superhuman' vision to inspect NASA's asteroid crash site
items.blurb: Around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) was by pretty much all measures a resounding success when it struck the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos going more than 22,000 kilometers per hour (13,700 miles per hour). However, we still don't know just how much of a success it actually was—DART was a one-way mission with no real way to track the results of the impact close up.

items.title: If tiny 'primordial' black holes exist, here's how we might find them
items.blurb: Scientists have hypothesized that, in the fraction of a second following the Big Bang, minute black holes may have been forged within tiny, dense pockets that collapsed under their own gravity. If these primordial black holes are ever found, they could represent a significant component of dark matter—the invisible substance that makes up most of the universe's matter.

items.title: The snake with a built-in egg peeler
items.blurb: Dr. Arthur Tiutenko from FAU and colleagues from LMU München and the South African National Museum in Bloemfontein discovered a new species of snake in the Harenna Forest, on the southern slopes of Ethiopia's Bale Mountains: Dasypeltis albigularis, or the white-throated egg-eater. "Three other new species in this genus are still waiting in line," the zoologist adds.

items.title: How a tiny chemical mark on a protein can be placed to double gene activity
items.blurb: Tiny chemical marks on histones—the proteins that package our DNA—can profoundly influence gene activity without changing the underlying DNA sequence. One such mark, known as histone acetylation, plays a crucial role in regulating gene expression and is frequently disrupted in diseases such as cancer. Researchers, however, wondered how the enzymes responsible for adding these marks know exactly where to place them.

items.title: Lonely shoppers demonstrate less compassion in their purchases than others, study shows
items.blurb: Chronically lonely people are less likely to buy products that benefit others, such as fair-trade or child-labor-free goods, according to a new study by researchers at Concordia and the University of the Fraser Valley. The team ran four studies involving more than 1,400 participants across North America. Each person completed a standard loneliness questionnaire, then chose between ordinary products and versions that cost 15% to 20% more but carried an ethical or environmental label. Items included toothpaste, chocolate bars, jackets and backpacks.

items.title: Light-activated nanoparticles may help treat head and neck cancer
items.blurb: For patients with head and neck cancer, treatment can come at a high cost to their quality of life, affecting their ability to speak, swallow and even breathe due to invasive procedures. Now, Penn State researchers have developed a light-activated nanoparticle system with the long-term goal of shrinking tumors while limiting exposure to healthy tissue and improving patients' quality of life after cancer treatment. Penn State has licensed the technology to Illuminate Therapeutics, which is advancing its preclinical development.

items.title: Ethiopian volcano's mysterious methane outburst may have a culprit—magma that never erupted
items.blurb: Experts were puzzled when satellite observations showed a volcano in Ethiopia emitting huge quantities of methane despite not erupting, but a team of researchers led by the University of Bristol believe they have discovered why this happened—and their findings could have implications for historical climate change research.

items.title: Ahead of Giving Tuesday, study finds charitable giving often misses communities with greatest need
items.blurb: As Giving Tuesday approaches, a recent study led by a University of Massachusetts Amherst public policy researcher finds that communities with greater economic disadvantage typically see less private charitable giving—despite having greater needs in many cases.

items.title: Gene variant gives male malaria mosquitoes a mating edge in the heat
items.blurb: Mosquitoes play a major role in spreading malaria, and understanding how they adapt to climate change is important for improving malaria prevention and control.

items.title: Cichlid sibling rivalry: Young fish fight more in some species than others
items.blurb: Though we may fight with our siblings sometimes, for most people a sibling is a constant companion throughout childhood and often for one's entire life. Yet this is not always the case in the animal kingdom: in some species, siblings engage in serious fights that can even escalate to fratricide. They may be genetically related, but must also compete for limited resources.

items.title: Rethinking the 'girls are worse with money' myth
items.blurb: New research led by Dr. Stephen Agnew from Te Whare Wānanga o Waitaha | University of Canterbury's (UC) Department of Economics and Finance is challenging one of the most persistent assumptions in education and everyday culture: that teenage girls are less financially literate than boys.

items.title: Remote jobs diminish hiring bias against mothers
items.blurb: The "motherhood penalty"—a workplace bias that assumes mothers are less committed to their careers, resulting in fewer opportunities, lower pay and slower advancement—could be reduced by shifting jobs from in-person to remote, according to new research by Claire Daviss, assistant professor of organizational behavior at the ILR School.

items.title: Optical DNA mapping assembles yeast genomes at chromosome scale
items.blurb: Large, complex genomes remain difficult to characterize accurately, even with modern DNA sequencing. Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology have now extended an optical genome mapping approach, previously demonstrated for bacterial genomes, to more complex eukaryotic genomes. Using two yeast species, they generated optical maps covering entire chromosomes, including large repetitive regions that are particularly difficult to reconstruct.

items.title: How Future Lunar Colonists Can Farm Potatoes on the Moon

items.title: How Our Eyes Betray Us When We Lie
items.blurb: Subtle shifts in gaze can signal we’re hiding something

items.title: Tiny, threadlike connections act as ‘skyways’ between cells
items.blurb: When a young researcher suggested cells trade resources through microscopic pipelines, many colleagues refused to believe it. Two decades later, these tunneling nanotubes are being studied for roles in cancer and other diseases.
